 Obesity is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease and stroke.
 Approximately 35% of adults in the US are obese.
 There are now more obese people in the world than there are undernourished.
 Obesity seems to have become a major issue in the nutrition world, but what actually is obesity?

 Obesity is usually diagnosed through BMI calculations. 

 Body Mass Index, or BMI, was released in the 1970’s by the CDC, or the Center for Disease Control. This was a quick, simple way to classify obesity. It is indirectly related to body fat. It measures the mass of a person (weight) and roughly divides it by the square of the height.

 BMI calculations can be performed by finding your weight (in kilograms) divided by the square of your height (in centimeters).

 There are ranges for BMI for adults, generally determined as follows:

 Underweight = < 18.5
 Normal weight = 18.5–24.9
 Overweight = 25–29.9
 Obese = BMI of 30 or greater

BMI is a common metric used to establish an individual as obese or overweight. The latest statistics published on the Sitepoint Blog, however, mentions that BMI can skew depending on the regions and cultures, and height is not taken into consideration.
